The winning answers in each requirement open with Cedar Prairie's own facts (Drupal 9, 3,400 pages, 900 PDFs, rate filings, Akamai, Compliance approval, Genesys, Salesforce FSC, Power BI) and then give named deliverables with sign-off and an hour estimate. Answers made of Adobe product description followed by a prerequisites list commit to nothing the panel could hold a vendor to.

Several answers hedge on choices the RFP already made: 'Adobe's managed CDN or your own' when Akamai is mandated, generic 'CRM' and 'BI tools' when Salesforce and Power BI are named, and commerce 'purchase' measures for an insurer.

F.3's strongest answer leaves an unfilled placeholder for the support hours the RFP explicitly asked for. Extra licenses (Workfront, Marketo Qualifier, CJA Prime) appear in otherwise strong answers, and the panel would want them priced in G.

Every answer is within its section's word limit, so length never separated them. Several strong answers do have short 'How we would do it' sections that leave out one requested element (the rollback steps in B.8, the off-site steps in C.2, the Salesforce-to-CJA steps in D.3), which only appears in their deliverables.

The one outlier is C.1 C at 128 hours for CTA click tracking alone. Several answers that describe far more work keep the same 32-hour figure (A.5 B).

The strongest answers used Tallgrass's own facts (2.4 million visits, 1,200 pages, the old in-house CMS, Snowflake, loyalty ID coverage, Power BI) and added verification steps: URL crawls and recrawls, reconciliation against Snowflake, number checks against Analysis Workspace, readiness sign-offs.

Adobe product statements were mostly specific and plausible (stage sized like production, permanent region choice, Data Mirror change data capture, the BI extension's limits, the Select and Prime stitching tiers). There were real slips: 'uses Adobe Analytics, licensed separately' in B.6, a stitching prerequisite attached to click tracking, and editable templates paired with the Universal Editor. Common gaps were SEO beyond redirects (sitemaps, canonicals, Search Console), Power BI Service refresh, and support response times. A.3 (migration) and Section D were not in the panel set.

scores.why: A ties the setup to our not-yet-provisioned state and nine-month plan, names single sign-on through our identity provider and flags the permanent region choice as the real risk; B is a sound but generic checklist with a confusing claim that our program is already 'ready'; C is one sentence plus off-topic after-launch work, with no deliverables, effort or risk.

C starts from our developer-for-every-change problem and our 1,200 pages and gives a signed-off component matrix, template policies and approved styles; A is a competent but generic build plan; B does not describe the build at all and talks about training and Cloud Manager instead.

B is the only answer that really protects our search rankings at our traffic level (full crawl, title and meta inventory, a 301 map we sign off, tested redirects, a recrawl after launch); C covers Adobe's go-live checklist well but treats SEO as just 'redirects for retired URLs'; A is mostly boilerplate about discovery, with one go-live sentence.

B targets our goal of no developer help, with workshops on real Tallgrass pages, an unaided publish test per author and office hours after launch; A is a reasonable generic training plan with no proof of readiness; C is a single sentence of product description that does not answer the question.

A designs around our Snowflake store and loyalty data and the new web feed, with a shared customer ID, a sample month in a development sandbox and checks of sales totals against Snowflake; C is a sound generic plan padded with call center and app channels we do not have; B drifts into audiences from AI-referred visits and licensing notes.

C sees that our loyalty ID is what links web visits to store purchases and measures how many web visits carry it before promising stitching, though its method stops before the data views; B is a complete but generic process; A is one sentence plus a licensing line repeated twice.

C names the questions our marketing and merchandising teams would actually ask (campaigns that lead to store purchases, online versus in-store category sales) and checks the numbers against Snowflake before sign-off; A is a tidy generic process with optional mobile scorecards; B is one hedged paragraph.

B is written for our executives in Power BI, with a dashboard specification, named owners, the 50,000-row and 30-day limits designed in, and hours broken out; C is a decent generic BI connection plan that lists executive dashboards without saying how they get built; A lists every BI tool plus Excel and offers one sentence of method.

notes: Every requirement had a clear winner that drew on our own situation: the 2.4 million monthly visits, the twelve-year-old custom CMS, the developer bottleneck, Snowflake, Power BI, the loyalty ID, 86 stores. The weaker answers could have been sent to any retailer.

One boilerplate sentence about 'your call center, point-of-sale systems and online properties' opens many of the weaker CJA answers. We have no call center in scope, so it reads as pasted text and lowers credibility.

Several answers were fragments, a single sentence or off-topic: go-live text pasted into C.2, training and Cloud Manager in answer to the A.2 build question, AI-referred audiences in B.1, after-launch work in A.1. Answers like these would be scored as non-responsive.

Licensing lines were often misplaced or repeated: a stitching prerequisite on a click-tracking answer, 'Adobe Analytics, which is licensed separately' in CJA training, a package line given twice. They suggest assembly from parts rather than understanding.

Weaker answers fell back on 'This runs during the build. It fits within your nine-month plan.' The stronger ones sequenced the work against its dependencies (after component sign-off, after data views, month nine). Several answers also listed deliverables, such as a pilot, data views or executive dashboards, that their method never described. All answers appeared to be within the 250-word limit.
